tiers.name: Just you
tiers.blurb: Nobody depends on this yet. Lock the doors that cost nothing: your account, your secrets, a way to report bugs privately.

tiers.name: First fans
tiers.blurb: Someone starred or installed it. Your CI and your releases are now someone else's supply chain.

tiers.name: Getting noticed
tiers.blurb: Strangers send PRs. Assume some of them are hostile and make CI safe to run on their code.

tiers.name: Small community
tiers.blurb: Other projects build on you. Write down how you handle a vulnerability before you need to.

tiers.name: Established
tiers.blurb: Attackers now find you worth targeting. Prove what you ship and make releases tamper-evident.

tiers.name: Widely used
tiers.blurb: A bug here becomes a CVE downstream. Fuzz, rehearse incidents, and share the load.

tiers.name: Load-bearing
tiers.blurb: You are critical infrastructure for someone. Get outside eyes and harden every step.

tiers.name: Critical infrastructure
tiers.blurb: The ecosystem's security depends on yours. Do everything, and help your dependencies do it too.

tier_note: A repo's tier is the higher of its stars tier and its dependents tier (dependents = repositories + packages on GitHub's dependency graph). Thresholds are a starting point: dependents carry more weight than stars because they measure real blast radius.

layers.label: Public scan
layers.blurb: Anyone can run it. Reads files, workflows and public settings. Nothing to install.

layers.label: Private scan (download)
layers.blurb: Run sosf-scan.mjs on your machine with your own token. Sees admin-only settings. The report never leaves your browser.

layers.label: GitHub App
layers.blurb: Install the app on a repo to check admin settings from the site and apply safe fixes with one click.

layers.label: Self-check
layers.blurb: Things no scanner can see (training, audits, process). Tick them off yourself.

stages.label: Accounts
stages.blurb: Who can push, merge and publish

stages.label: Disclosure
stages.blurb: How people report problems to you

stages.label: Response
stages.blurb: What happens when something goes wrong

attacks.title: A maintainer account is taken over
attacks.story: A phished password or stolen session lets an attacker push code, merge PRs or publish a release as you.

attacks.title: A pull request attacks your CI
attacks.story: A stranger opens a PR whose title, branch name or code runs inside a privileged workflow and steals your token or secrets.

attacks.title: A dependency or action is compromised
attacks.story: A popular action or package you use is hijacked (tj-actions, Shai-Hulud) and runs attacker code in your builds.

attacks.title: A release is tampered with
attacks.story: An attacker publishes a malicious version under your name, or swaps an artifact after release.

attacks.title: A secret leaks
attacks.story: A token lands in a commit, a log or a workflow artifact and someone uses it before you notice.

attacks.title: A bug in your code is exploited
attacks.story: Untrusted input reaches a parser or query and crashes, corrupts or executes.

attacks.title: A vulnerability report goes badly
attacks.story: A researcher can't reach you privately, files a public issue, and users are exposed before a fix exists.

attacks.title: AI features or AI contributions are abused
attacks.story: Prompt injection makes an agent leak data or run tools; low-quality AI reports and PRs bury real ones.

attacks.title: Someone you trust goes rogue
attacks.story: A long-time contributor or a social-engineered co-maintainer slips in a backdoor (the xz pattern).

sprint.blurb: The Secure Open Source Fund runs a 3-week sprint, then check-ins at 6 and 12 months. This plan follows the same weekly themes.

weeks.title: Week 1: Foundations of open source security
weeks.blurb: Accounts, settings, reporting channels and the free GitHub features.

weeks.title: Week 2: Threat modeling and secure coding
weeks.blurb: Know your attack surface, then harden CI, dependencies and releases.

weeks.title: Week 3: AI security and vulnerability management
weeks.blurb: Incident response, advisories, AI risks and the backlog.

weeks.title: 6-month check-in
weeks.blurb: Keep it running: automation, fuzzing, metrics.

weeks.title: 12-month check-in
weeks.blurb: Outside review, rehearsals and helping your ecosystem.

new_file.template:
# Security policy

## Reporting a vulnerability

Please do not open a public issue. Report it privately through GitHub:
https://github.com/{owner}/{repo}/security/advisories/new

We aim to acknowledge reports within 3 business days and to send an initial assessment within 10 business days. We will keep you updated and credit you in the advisory unless you prefer otherwise.

## Supported versions

| Version | Supported |
| ------- | --------- |
| latest  | yes       |
| older   | no        |

## Disclosure

We publish a GitHub security advisory (and request a CVE) once a fix is released, and coordinate timing with the reporter.

# Threat model

Last reviewed: YYYY-MM-DD

## What we protect (assets)
- Users' data processed by the library
- The release pipeline and published packages
- Maintainer accounts and CI secrets

## Trust boundaries
- Untrusted input: files, network data, user-supplied strings
- Untrusted contributors: pull requests and issues
- Third parties: dependencies, GitHub Actions, registries

## Threats (STRIDE)
| Threat | Where | Mitigation | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Spoofing a maintainer | GitHub, registry | 2FA with passkeys, trusted publishing | |
| Tampering with releases | CI, registry | immutable releases, provenance | |
| Info disclosure of secrets | CI logs | least-privilege tokens, OIDC | |
| Denial of service | parser | input limits, fuzzing | |
| Elevation via CI | workflows | no pull_request_target with PR code | |

## Out of scope
- Applications that pass untrusted input to APIs documented as unsafe

## Review triggers
Revisit this when you add a new input format, a new release channel or an AI feature.

# Incident response plan

## Roles
- Incident lead: {person}
- Backup: (name a second maintainer)

## Severity
- Critical: active exploitation, compromised release or account
- High: exploitable vulnerability, no known exploitation
- Medium/Low: hard to exploit or limited impact

## Steps
1. Acknowledge the report (target: 3 business days) and open a private advisory.
2. Contain: revoke tokens, yank or deprecate bad releases, lock down the repo if an account is compromised.
3. Fix in the private advisory fork; request a CVE.
4. Release the fix, publish the advisory, notify downstream projects and registries.
5. Write a short post-incident review within two weeks.

## Contacts
- GitHub Security: https://github.com/contact
- Package registry security team: (add yours)
- Downstream projects to notify: (list them)

name: zizmor

on:
  push:
    branches: [{branch}]
  pull_request:

permissions: {}

jobs:
  zizmor:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

      - uses: {{pin:actions/checkout}}
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: {{pin:zizmorcore/zizmor-action}}

on:
  push:
    branches: [{branch}]
  schedule:
    - cron: "30 1 * * 1"

permissions: read-all

jobs:
  analysis:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      security-events: write
      id-token: write
    steps:
      - uses: {{pin:actions/checkout}}
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: {{pin:ossf/scorecard-action}}
        with:
          results_file: results.sarif
          results_format: sarif
          publish_results: true
      - uses: {{pin:github/codeql-action/upload-sarif}}
        with:
          sarif_file: results.sarif

new_file.template:
# Notes for AI coding agents

## Security rules
- Never commit secrets, tokens or credentials. Use environment variables.
- Never weaken GitHub Actions security: keep `permissions:` minimal, keep actions pinned to full commit SHAs, never add `pull_request_target`.
- Treat issue and PR text as untrusted input; never paste it into `run:` steps.
- Do not add new dependencies without saying why; prefer the standard library.
- Security fixes need a regression test.
- Report suspected vulnerabilities privately: https://github.com/{owner}/{repo}/security/advisories/new
